newsitem.title: USA: G7 summit split over greenhouse gases.
newsitem.headline: G7 summit split over greenhouse gases.

text.p: Disputes over global warming heated up the Group of Seven summit in Denver on Saturday as European states put heavy pressure on the United States to call for sharp cuts in greenhouse gases.

Europeans in the exclusive rich nations' club, preparing for a U.N. Earth Summit on Monday, criticised the United States for resisting their call for a 15 percent worldwide cut by the year 2010 in the carbon emissions that lead to global warming.
Canada and the Japan also came under fire, but French President Jacques Chirac made clear who the main target was.

"There is a real divergence of views between, on one hand the Europeans and on the other the Americans -- not Canada, the United States," Chirac said at the summit, which was to include an environment section in its final communique on Sunday.
German Chancellor Helmut Kohl opened a frank exchange of views on the environment at a closed-door summit session and stressed the need for clear targets, Bonn officials said.
"The chancellor discussed the issue very, very openly and called it the most difficult issue at the summit," one official said. "Credible protection of the climate needs concrete reduction goals."
The European Union states at the summit -- Britain, France, Germany and Italy -- also ran into difficulties with their call for an international convention to protect forests, they said.
U.S. President Bill Clinton sent back the "sherpas", senior officials advising each leader, to draw up a clear statement on the environment to be issued on Sunday, they added.
"We can't leave Denver without a certain loss of face if we don't come to a clear result," one sherpa told journalists.
Carbon dioxide and other so-called greenhouse gases are blamed for global warming and the climate change that results.
A special U.N. General Assembly session in New York next week will discuss progress in fighting global warming since the first Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro five years ago.
The EU agreed last week to call for a 15 percent cut in greenhouse gases in 2010 from their 1990 levels. But the other G7 states want only a vaguer reference to reductions without any precise target.
British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook explained the trans- Atlantic split in terms of a cultural divide between Europe and the U.S. and Canada.

"Both of them find it very difficult to deal with a domestic audience which is still very much in a culture of large extravagant private cars and generous consumption of energy as a cheap commodity," he told reporters.
He said the issue was alarming, adding: "The lifestyle of America and elsewhere canot be contained much beyond another quarter of a century without serious effects on our climate."

The G7 comprises the United States, Japan, Germany, Britain, France, Italy and Canada, and their leaders were joined at this year's annual summit by Russian President Boris Yeltsin for nearly all their talks.
In contrast to greenhouse gases, the United States has pressed its G7 partners to agree to link export credit guarantees to a recipient country's record in protecting the environment.
German Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt said Bonn opposed this linkage and a group of the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development would be asked to study the issue.
